Good morning—thank you for making time today. I’m Claire, a perinatal mental-health clinician who works with new mothers. Over the next few minutes I’ll be guiding you through a short tool called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS. It’s simply a 10-question check-in about how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived, and it helps us catch anything from the normal “baby blues” to something that might need extra support. Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me someone is in danger. We’ll go one question at a time, and you can answer in your own words—no right or wrong answers. Ready to start?

In the past seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly? Not much. I used to laugh all the time—little things would crack me up—but lately it’s like the switch is stuck in the “off” position. Maybe once or twice this week my husband made a joke and I managed half a smile, but it felt forced. Most of the day I’m too tired or worried to find anything funny.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Not very often. I can’t remember the last time I really laughed—maybe a quiet chuckle when the baby made a silly face, but even that felt flat. It’s like the joy is stuck behind a wall of exhaustion and worry.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I used to get excited about little plans—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just watching a show I liked—but now it all feels like another chore. I still try to set up small things, thinking “maybe this will feel good,” but when the time comes I’m too tired or anxious and I just want to stay home.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… that one hits. Yesterday the baby wouldn’t nap and I kept thinking it must be something I’m doing—maybe I’m not swaddling right or I waited too long to put him down. I ended up crying in the nursery, telling myself I’m a terrible mom. Even when my husband says it’s normal baby stuff, my brain still circles back to “this is my fault.”
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure she’s not gaining enough weight, or I’ll lie awake picturing her tiny chest not moving. There’s no real reason—her check-ups have been fine—but the thoughts just barge in and I can’t swat them away for hours.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes—most days. Sometimes my chest gets tight and my thoughts spiral about whether I'm feeding right, sleeping enough, or just "what-ifs" about her breathing, the flat, racing heartbeat - quantitative findings up front

Things have been getting on top of me

Yes. Most days it feels like I’m drowning in small tasks—one bottle, one diaper, one burp cloth at a time—and suddenly the whole day is gone and I still haven’t showered or eaten a real meal. I’ll be rocking the baby and think, “I can’t do this,” even though I’m already doing it. It’s like my mind is running a marathon while my body’s stuck in quicksand.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah, that’s been happening. After the night feeds I lie there staring at the ceiling, running through everything I might have messed up—did I sterilize the bottles right, am I producing enough milk, is she too hot, too cold… the thoughts just loop. I finally drift off maybe an hour before she wakes again, so most mornings I feel like I’ve barely slept at all even when the baby’s been settled.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day this week. It’s like there’s a gray cloud parked over me—sometimes lighter, sometimes heavier, but always there. I’ll be changing her diaper and tears just start leaking out, or I’ll catch myself staring out the window feeling empty. I keep telling myself I should be grateful, but the sadness still sits heavy in my chest.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yes… most days. I’ll be rocking her and suddenly my eyes just well up. Sometimes it’s because I feel useless, sometimes I don’t even know why—it just spills out. Yesterday my husband found me sobbing over a pile of clean laundry because I couldn’t get it folded “right.” He kept saying it’s okay, but I couldn’t stop the tears.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I feel low and overwhelmed, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel like me again so I can be the mom my baby deserves.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  

Date: [today]  
Respondent: 0–6 mo postpartum mother (infant 2–4 mo per narrative)  
Tool: 10-item Edinburgh Plus Anxiety Probe  

A. Positive Screening Items (≥ 1 = present)  
- Anhedonia: marked loss of pleasure/humor (Q1, Q2)  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame (Q3)  
- Generalized anxiety & panic without clear trigger (Q4, Q5)  
- Feeling overwhelmed / unable to cope (Q6)  
- Mood-linked insomnia (Q7)  
- Persistent sadness/crying spells (Q8, Q9)  

B. Safety Item  
- Self-harm ideation: denied (Q10) → no acute SI reported  

C. Pattern Summary  
Daily low mood, anhedonia, prominent guilt, intrusive worry, somatic anxiety (tight chest, racing heart), and functional impairment (self-care, household tasks) persisting ≥ 2 wk; sleep disruption driven by rumination rather than infant schedule alone.  

D. Risk Factors Identified  
- Postpartum period (hormonal, role transition stress)  
- Primiparous self-critical cognitions (“terrible mom”)  
- Anxiety-depression symptom cluster (possible comorbidity)  

E. Screening Conclusion  
Meets screening threshold for probable major postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety; denies self-harm. Recommend formal diagnostic assessment and safety plan today.
